md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong (false sharing).

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: The longer sequence costs compute. Linear layers scale with token count, so 577 vs 197 tokens is about 2.9x more work per layer, while the attention score matrix grows with the square, about $(577/197)^2 \approx 8.6$x. Simplified: real step time also depends on kernels and memory traffic. Higher-resolution fine-tuning trades accuracy for a large jump in cost.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching
md: pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
md: A backend is mostly a *declaration*: what it supports, plus two factories. Selection, batching, KV layout and CUDA graph capture are all driven by those declarations, so a backend never needs to know about the scheduler.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the image at full resolution. It sees whatever grid the encoder produced. A 4000 x 3000 phone photo squeezed into 336 x 336 loses most of its pixels before the language model ever runs.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Why a lock-free CAS loop can starve one thread
md: The progress ladder, weakest to strongest: **blocking** (a stalled lock holder can stop everyone), **lock-free** (some thread always completes), **wait-free** (every thread completes in finitely many of its own steps), **bounded wait-free** (every thread completes within a fixed number of its own steps).

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: A common misconception is that these models learn from raw observations. They learn to imitate ERA5, so they inherit its biases (GraphCast excludes precipitation from its headline evaluation because ERA5 precipitation has known biases), and they start each forecast from an NWP analysis.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Common failure modes: modifying a buffer or file before the kernel is done with it (silent corruption on the wire), forgetting to drain the error queue (pinned memory grows until ENOBUFS), benchmarking over loopback (always copied), and assuming a notification means the peer received the data.
